question: How does mini-batch stochasticity select qualitatively different global minima when a single-neuron autoencoder is trained on orthogonal data?

key_findings.claim: Full-batch gradient descent converges to a dense global minimum aligned with the projected initialization.
key_findings.evidence: For the linear tied-weight autoencoder on orthonormal samples, symmetry preserves relative coordinates and the limit is the normalized projection of the initial weight onto the data span. Under random initialization it spreads over many examples and has high cosine similarity with its initial direction.

key_findings.claim: Any fixed batch size strictly below the dataset size almost surely selects a one-sparse data direction under the stated random sampling and step-size conditions.
key_findings.evidence: Random batches break the full-batch coordinate symmetry; a non-homogeneous random-walk argument shows one positive coordinate eventually dominates and the normalized iterate converges to a single example. The phase boundary is discontinuous at full batch in this ideal orthogonal problem.

key_findings.claim: The same dense-versus-sparse distinction extends to a ReLU single-neuron autoencoder after restricting to initially active orthogonal examples.
key_findings.evidence: For Gaussian initialization exact orthogonality occurs with probability zero. Full batch converges to a dense combination over the active set, whereas mini-batch SGD converges to one active data vector, under bounded initialization and constant step size.

key_findings.claim: In this model small-batch SGD reaches sharper, not flatter, minima by Hessian trace, undermining a universal batch-size-to-flatness narrative.
key_findings.evidence: The maximum Hessian eigenvalue does not distinguish the two solution types, while the trace ranks the one-sparse SGD minima as sharper than the dense GD minima. Both are global training minima; the result shows sharpness depends on model, metric, and parameterization rather than refuting empirical large-batch effects generally.

method.core_idea: Solve the stochastic coordinate dynamics exactly enough to see which member of a non-unique global-minimum manifold each batch regime selects.
method.mechanism: Express weights in an orthonormal data basis, derive coordinate recurrences for full and mini-batch updates, prove boundedness and convergence, analyze the ratio process as a non-homogeneous random walk, extend active-set reasoning to ReLU, and calculate Hessian spectra at limiting solutions.
assumptions: A single tied-weight neuron is trained on exactly orthogonal samples.
Initialization norm and constant step size satisfy stability bounds.
Mini-batches are sampled with the stated randomness.
Sparsity in the training-data basis is a useful proxy for feature selection.
Distance from initialization is a useful proxy for feature learning.

techniques.role: Decouples autoencoder updates into interpretable coefficients.
Proves stochastic symmetry breaking and winner selection.
Extends linear results to a ReLU neuron.
Compares equally optimal but geometrically different limits.
Tests trace and top-eigenvalue notions of sharpness.

evaluations.setting: Linear one-neuron autoencoder on m orthonormal samples
evaluations.result: Full batch yields a dense initialization-aligned minimum; every b<m yields a one-sparse data vector
The dense-versus-one-sparse split persists under stated conditions

evaluations.metric: Cosine to initialization and data vectors
evaluations.result: GD changes features little; SGD becomes nearly orthogonal to initialization and aligned to one datum in high dimension
Top eigenvalue ties; trace labels small-batch minima sharper
evaluations.baseline: Common claim that smaller batches prefer flatter minima

limitations: The data are exactly orthogonal and the model has one neuron.
The selected one-example feature is not necessarily useful generalization or dictionary recovery.
Constant-step asymptotic results may not describe decayed practical training.
No empirical deep-autoencoder or natural-data test accompanies the theory.
failure_modes: Correlated samples couple coordinates and remove the sharp phase boundary.
Multiple neurons divide or duplicate winning features.
Momentum or adaptive scaling changes the random-walk drift.
Batch sampling without replacement has different long-run dependence.
A decaying step freezes a mixed solution before winner selection.
Sparse selection overfits one example rather than a latent source.
reusable_insights: Analyze optimizer bias on a manifold of equal-loss solutions rather than only convergence rate.
Separate sparsity, distance from initialization, and sharpness as distinct implicit biases.
Check whether a claimed batch-size law survives alternative sharpness definitions.
Look for stochastic symmetry breaking at the full-batch boundary.
Extend solvable models incrementally to correlated data and multiple features.
open_questions: What replaces one-sparse winner selection for incoherent or sparse-coding data?
How do multiple neurons allocate features under different batch sizes?
Does momentum preserve or weaken stochastic symmetry breaking?
Can finite-time theory predict the selected feature before asymptotic convergence?
Which geometry correlates with generalization when Hessian sharpness reverses?

competitive_landscape.title: On Large-Batch Training for Deep Learning: Generalization Gap and Sharp Minima
competitive_landscape.difference: Keskar et al. associate large batches with sharp minima and poorer generalization in deep networks. This paper provides a solvable counterexample where small-batch minima have larger Hessian trace, showing the association is not universal.

competitive_landscape.title: From Principal Subspaces to Principal Components with Linear Autoencoders
competitive_landscape.difference: Plaut clarifies what linear autoencoders identify about PCA subspaces. The reviewed paper focuses on which member of a degenerate solution set is selected by batch stochasticity in a tied one-neuron setting.

competitive_landscape.title: (S)GD over Diagonal Linear Networks: Implicit Bias, Large Stepsizes and Edge of Stability
competitive_landscape.difference: Even et al. analyze how stochasticity and large steps change implicit regularization in diagonal networks. This paper finds an especially sharp full-versus-mini-batch sparsity transition in autoencoder coordinates.

competitive_landscape.title: Sharp Minima Can Generalize For Deep Nets
competitive_landscape.difference: Dinh et al. show parameter rescaling can change sharpness without changing function. The current result adds a metric-dependent reversal even within one fixed toy parameterization, reinforcing caution about flatness narratives.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Mini-batch stochasticity provably induces sparse feature selection and a discontinuous implicit bias at full batch in a nonconvex autoencoder, while reversing the usual sharpness story.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Exact convergence theorems cover linear and ReLU cases, a new random-walk argument proves winner selection, and Hessian spectra characterize limiting minima.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The solvable phase transition and proof tool are novel and crisp. Their importance lies as a counterexample and mechanism, not as direct evidence that practical autoencoders or deep networks behave the same way.

reviewer_notes: Read all 48 extracted pages, including linear and ReLU theorems, random-walk proof, sharpness calculation, conclusion, and appendices. Four primary arXiv competitors were checked on 2026-08-23. Theorems were passage-checked structurally; constants were not independently rederived.
